Boundary conditions
What can happen when the material changes?
Return to the gap and replace part of its
ﬁlling with a diﬀerent material. The space remains connected, but the material response changes
at an internal surface. A ﬁeld component may now jump as we cross it. Which jumps are possible,
and which would contradict the laws we have just learned?
A boundary condition answers that question by relating the two sides of the interface.
Some
components must be continuous; other jumps are supported by surface charge or current. We can
discover the rules by taking our familiar loops and closed surfaces and making them very thin
across the boundary.
The ﬁelds labelled 1 and 2 below mean the limiting values just next to the same interface point
on the two sides. They are not values at two widely separated locations. In the bulk of either
material, ordinary spatial derivatives can be used. At an ideal sharp jump, shrinking integral loops
and volumes provide the appropriate description without treating the ﬁeld as diﬀerentiable across
that jump.
There is one normal direction but an entire tangent plane.
Choose the unit normal ˆn
from medium 1 into medium 2. At a ﬂat interface we can also choose two perpendicular unit
tangents ˆt1, ˆt2. Any vector Fi just inside medium i, where i = 1 or 2, can be separated as
Fin = Fi · ˆn,
Fin = Fin ˆn,
Fit = Fi −Fin ˆn.
Fin is a signed scalar; Fin is its normal vector. The tangential part Fit is also a vector, with two
independent components. Its subscript t means “tangential”, not time. The time argument, when
needed, is written in parentheses.

Two projection tests appear in the equations.
A dot product with ˆn selects the one normal
component. A cross product with ˆn eliminates the normal component and tests the tangential
part. Thus ˆn × (F2 −F1) = 0 means both tangential components agree, not that the full vectors
agree. Both normal components must use the same ˆn, rather than separate outward normals for
the two materials.
Tangential electric ﬁeld: shrink the height of a loop.
Cut the interface along a chosen
unit tangent ˆt, and make a rectangular loop in the plane containing ˆt and ˆn. Let ℓbe its long-side
length and h its height across the interface. These are distances, not ﬁeld quantities. Traverse the
top edge in medium 2 along +ˆt, and the bottom edge in medium 1 along −ˆt.

For bounded volume-

concentrated within a layer of vanishing thickness but has a ﬁnite integrated strength Js. That
strength is measured in A/m, meaning amperes crossing each metre of a cut through the sheet,
not A/m2.

Why some terms disappear and others do not
A bounded volume density integrated through a layer of thickness h gives a contribution
proportional to h; it vanishes as the layer shrinks. A surface density is already an integral
through the thin layer, so its contribution is proportional to face area or cut length and
remains ﬁnite. This is why ρs and Js survive the limiting arguments while ordinary bounded
bulk densities do not.
Charge conservation at the interface.
The interface charge is not an arbitrary correction
added to Gauss’s law. It can accumulate when the arriving conduction current diﬀers from the
departing current. For a patch of area A, current can also spread sideways within the interface.
With no lateral current, the balance is simply

All current components use ˆn from 1 to 2. The units agree: ∂tρs and Jin both have units A/m2.
For a general sheet current, let u, v be perpendicular distance coordinates within a locally ﬂat
tangent plane. Its surface divergence ∇s · Js = ∂Jsu/∂u + ∂Jsv/∂v measures the net sideways
current leaving per unit interface area. Including this path gives
∂ρs
∂t + ∇s · Js + ˆn · (J2 −J1) = 0.
(1.39)
If both charge accumulation and surface-current divergence vanish, then J1n = J2n. More generally,
the normal currents match whenever ∂tρs + ∇s · Js = 0; the two terms can cancel even if neither
vanishes separately. In a transient, unequal conduction currents are often exactly what creates the
surface charge required by the ﬁeld jump.
Two dielectrics: apply the assumptions separately.
A perfect dielectric in this model has
σ = 0: it carries no ohmic conduction current. That property does not erase a free charge that has
previously been placed on its surface. If an interface between two perfect dielectrics has ρs = 0
and Js = 0, the four relations are
E1t = E2t,
H1t = H2t,
D1n = D2n,
B1n = B2n.
Notice the pattern: tangential E, H; normal D, B. It follows from the type of integral used, not
from a rule that all components of a ﬁeld must match. If both media are nonmagnetic, meaning
µ1 = µ2 = µ0, the normal and tangential components of B are then all continuous.

A perfect electric conductor: how the surface supports exterior ﬁelds.
An ideal perfect
electric conductor (PEC) is the limit in which a nonzero bulk electric ﬁeld would require unbounded
conduction current. The bulk ﬁeld is taken as zero. Real conductors can have small electric ﬁelds,
ﬁnite losses, and ﬁnite penetration depths; these are outside the PEC idealisation.
An electric ﬁeld tangent to the exterior surface would equal the interior tangential ﬁeld by the
shrinking-loop argument. It must therefore vanish. A normal exterior electric ﬁeld can remain,
ending on the conductor’s surface charge.
Similarly, an exterior tangential magnetic ﬁeld can
remain and is supported by a surface current.

Worked example 1.21
Two lossy dielectric layers: interface charge during a transient
We can ﬁnally calculate how the two-layer version of the device settles. Here we broaden the open-
ing idealisation: the materials may conduct weakly, so leakage and interface-charge accumulation
are allowed. “Lossy” refers to that nonzero conductivity in this model. The question is how the
ﬁeld in each layer adjusts while the applied voltage stays ﬁxed.
A parallel-plate capacitor has area A and plate separation 2d. Each of two layers has thickness d,
with constant properties (ε1, σ1) and (ε2, σ2). Use the electroquasistatic (lumped) model: the ﬁeld
redistribution across the device is treated as eﬀectively instantaneous on the relaxation time of
interest, so we neglect propagation delay, inductive voltage, and edge eﬀects. The model describes
the material relaxation after the unresolved switching event; it does not describe the microscopic
instant of applying an ideal voltage step. A voltage V0 is maintained across the plates for t > 0;
initially ρs(0+) = 0.
The unknowns are the two layer ﬁelds E1(t), E2(t) and the interface charge ρs(t). Three physical
statements determine them: the applied voltage ﬁxes the sum of the voltage drops, Gauss’s law
relates their normal displacements to surface charge, and charge conservation determines how that
charge changes. Equal thicknesses alone do not make the ﬁelds equal.
Choose the ﬁelds and the interface normal from layer 1 towards layer 2. The one-dimensional
ﬁelds are Ei = Ei ˆn. The scalar ﬁeld components Ei are measured along this normal, and the layer
voltage drops are dEi. The two relations needed ﬁrst are
d(E1 + E2) = V0,
ε2E2 −ε1E1 = ρs.
(1.41)
The ﬁrst is the total voltage drop; the second is electric Gauss’s law at the interface.

Initially the ﬁeld division is controlled by permittivity; at steady state it is controlled by conduc-

The mechanism is a feedback process. If J1 > J2, positive charge builds up at the interface. The
ﬁeld expressions show that this reduces E1 and increases E2, reducing the incoming current and
increasing the outgoing current until they agree. If the imbalance has the opposite sign, the charge
and ﬁeld changes reverse. If σ1ε2 = σ2ε1, the initial currents already match and no interface charge
develops from the speciﬁed initial state.

After time τ, the initial volume charge is reduced to 1/e of its original value. The units conﬁrm that

Worked example 1.23
Checking whether a proposed magnetic ﬁeld is possible
Consider B = κxt ˆz in a homogeneous medium, where κ is a ﬁxed coeﬃcient with units T/(m s).
It makes the units explicit; the numerical form Bz = xt corresponds to setting that coeﬃcient to
one in the chosen units. First, ∇· B = ∂z(κxt) = 0. Faraday’s law also requires ∇× E = −κxˆz.
One simple choice is
E = −κx2
2 ˆy,
because its only nonzero curl component is ∂x(−κx2/2) = −κx. Electric Gauss’s law gives ρ =
ε∇· E = 0.
Now H = κxtˆz/µ, so
∇× H = −κt
µ ˆy.
As ∂tD = 0, Ampère–Maxwell requires J = −(κt/µ)ˆy. Finally, ∇· J = 0 = −∂tρ, so continuity
also holds.
This supplies a consistent ﬁeld and source combination. Here J is a prescribed source current; the
example does not assert that this particular J and E satisfy a constant-conductivity Ohm’s law.
Verifying ∇· B = 0 alone would not have completed the check.
The choice of E is not unique from Faraday’s law alone: adding a suitable time-independent
gradient ﬁeld leaves its curl unchanged, while generally changing the charge required by Gauss’s
law. Specifying sources, material relations, initial conditions, and boundary conditions is what
turns consistency checks into a deﬁnite physical problem.
Worked example 1.24
A breathing charged sphere
A spherical conducting shell carries constant total charge Q, while its radius varies between rmin
and rmax. At any ﬁxed r > rmax, spherical symmetry gives a purely radial ﬁeld, and a concentric
Gaussian sphere always encloses Q. Thus
4πr2ε0Er(r, t) = Q
=⇒
E(r, t) =
Q
4πε0r2 ˆr .
The crucial steps were spherical symmetry and a constant enclosed total charge. Gauss’s law by
itself ﬁxes only a ﬂux integral; symmetry allowed us to replace the integral by 4πr2Er. There
is no time dependence at that exterior point. A changing radius by itself does not create the
proposed sinusoidally varying, spherically symmetric radial electric wave when the total charge
remains ﬁxed.
